strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: moving away from the unstructured, overlapping nature of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to an explicit Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) backbone directly targets the core issues of spatial ambiguity, alpha-blending artifacts, and heavy memory sorting bottlenecks during 3D feature registration.

Strong empirical performance: the proposed framework demonstrates substantial improvements on ScanNet open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation (+21.56% mIoU on 19 classes over Dr. Splat) and achieves leading results on LERF 3D object retrieval.

Efficiency benefits: by eliminating the need for multi-scale SAM proposal generations and replacing inverse volume rendering with deterministic confidence-gated voxel fusion, feature lifting time is reduced to ~3 minutes and preprocessing time is reduced by over 8x compared to hierarchical pipelines like LangSplat.

Thorough ablation study and analysis: the paper systematically evaluates each component (patch-wise depth/normal priors, TSDF confidence, AM-RADIO token usage, and sliding window upsampling with SCRA/SCGA filtering) and provides an insightful discussion on why learning-based upsamplers (e.g., AnyUp) degrade zero-shot cosine retrieval.
weaknesses: Disentanglement of gains: the framework introduces both a new geometric representation (SVRaster + depth/normal priors) and a stronger dense foundation model (AM-RADIO + SCRA/SCGA). It is somewhat unclear how much of the ScanNet gain stems from the AM-RADIO representation versus the SVRaster geometric backbone; evaluating 3DGS (e.g., Dr. Splat) augmented with the same AM-RADIO features would better isolate these contributions.

Component novelty: several core building blocks are direct adaptations from prior work (e.g., patch-depth normalization from DN-Gaussian, normal loss from MonoSDF, and SCRA/SCGA attention modules from RADSeg). The novelty is predominantly in the system integration and adaptation to SVRaster rather than standalone algorithmic inventions.

Minor formatting and reference errors: there is a broken reference in Section 4.3 ('in Figure ??'), inconsistent citations for Dr. Splat in Fig. 9 ([13] instead of [7]) and LangSplat in Table 7 ([21] instead of [19]), and the running header remains 'Abbreviated paper title'.

strengths: Well-motivated departure from unstructured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to explicit Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster), which resolves the spatial ambiguity and severe memory bottlenecks inherent in inverse volume rendering and direct Gaussian feature registration.
Bypassing the costly multi-level SAM mask extraction pipeline by leveraging the emergent dense language alignment of AM-RADIO patch tokens, achieving a notable ~8x speedup in preprocessing time.
Thoughtful geometric design incorporating patch-wise depth and normal priors along with a multi-level TSDF confidence weighting mechanism to gate 2D feature projection against surface discrepancies.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple tasks (LERF 3D/2D object retrieval, ScanNet open-vocabulary point cloud segmentation, and qualitative KITTI-360 editing) demonstrating substantial quantitative gains over prior registration and distillation baselines.
Clear ablation study validating the additive value of the geometric constraints, TSDF confidence map, sliding-window upsampling, and self-correcting attention filtering.
weaknesses: Confounding factors in baseline comparisons: LESV benefits significantly from the stronger AM-RADIO backbone (which distills DINOv2, SAM, and SigLIP), whereas key baselines like Dr. Splat and LangSplat rely on standard CLIP embeddings. An ablation or baseline comparison applying AM-RADIO features to 3DGS direct registration (or testing LESV with CLIP) is missing, making it hard to decouple the architectural voxel-fusion advantages from the superior 2D vision-language backbone.

High reliance on assembling existing components: the patch depth loss is adopted from DN-Gaussian, normal supervision from MonoSDF, SCRA/SCGA modules from RADSeg, and SVRaster from Sun et al. While their synergy in this domain is sound and well-engineered, the conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental.
Minor presentation flaws, such as a broken reference tag ('Figure ??') on page 12 of the manuscript.

strengths: Clear Motivation: Transitioning from unstructured, overlapping 3D Gaussian primitives to explicit, disjoint voxel representations (SVRaster) provides a sound conceptual motivation for eliminating alpha-blending ambiguities and spatial semantic bleeding in direct 3D feature lifting.

Efficiency Gains: The proposed direct volume fusion bypasses per-view Gaussian depth sorting and multi-level SAM mask extraction, reducing feature lifting time to ~3 minutes and per-scene preprocessing time to ~14 minutes (compared to ~120 minutes for LangSplat).

Comprehensive Benchmarking: The paper evaluates across several tasks and benchmarks, including 3D and 2D object retrieval on LERF, open-vocabulary point cloud segmentation on ScanNet, and qualitative demos on KITTI-360.

Insightful Upsampling Analysis: The ablation in Section 4.4 and Appendix A provides interesting observations on why learning-based deep feature upsamplers (e.g., AnyUp) harm zero-shot cosine similarity retrieval due to feature space homogenization.
weaknesses: Confounded Experimental Comparisons: The performance gains reported over baselines like Dr. Splat and LangSplat conflate the change in 3D representation (SVRaster vs. 3DGS) with the upgrade in the underlying 2D vision-language model (AM-RADIO + RADSeg attention vs. CLIP/OpenCLIP). To isolate the benefit of the structured voxel representation, the authors should evaluate Dr. Splat or Feature3DGS when supplied with the identical AM-RADIO dense features.

Limited Technical Novelty: The framework primarily orchestrates existing components: SVRaster as the underlying representation, standard monocular patch-depth and normal priors (from DN-Gaussian and MonoSDF), AM-RADIO as the foundation feature extractor, and SCRA/SCGA modules adopted directly from RADSeg. The individual algorithmic innovations introduced specifically in this work appear incremental.

Drafting Errors and Unresolved References: On page 12, Section 4.3, there is a broken LaTeX cross-reference ('...in Figure ??.'). In addition, several references and phrases (e.g., referencing hardware as 'featuring compute and VRAM capabilities equivalent to an NVIDIA RTX 5090') detract from the polish and rigor of the presentation.

Lack of Failure Case Analysis and Limitations: The manuscript does not discuss failure modes, sensitivity to voxel resolution vs. memory consumption trade-offs, or cases where explicit voxel grids struggle compared to Gaussian splats (e.g., thin structures, specularity, or novel-view rendering quality).

strengths: Principled paradigm shift from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding, which effectively eliminates spatial ambiguities, ray-like spillovers, and semantic bleeding inherent to overlapping anisotropic Gaussians.

Well-designed geometric regularization and feature lifting pipeline, specifically combining patch-wise depth and normal priors with an adaptive multi-level TSDF confidence weighting mechanism to gate multi-view feature projection.

Effective utilization of agglomerative foundation models (AM-RADIO), enabling multi-granularity part-to-whole open-vocabulary queries without the substantial computational overhead of hierarchical SAM mask extraction.

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks and tasks (ScanNet 3D segmentation, LERF 2D/3D object retrieval, KITTI-360), showing substantial improvements in 3D point cloud understanding (+21.56% mIoU on ScanNet-19 over Dr. Splat) and competitive retrieval accuracy.

Significant computational and memory advantages: deterministic spatial batching achieves O(1) memory scalability (~22.5 GB peak vs. >130 GB for 3DGS registration baselines) and slashes preprocessing/lifting time to ~17 minutes.
weaknesses: Several components are direct adaptations or combinations of prior techniques (e.g., patch-depth normalization from DN-Gaussian, normal loss from MonoSDF, and SCRA/SCGA filtering from RADSeg), which somewhat tempers the purely algorithmic novelty of the individual blocks despite the overall strong system synthesis.

Inheriting the limitations of direct feature registration methods, LESV stores high-dimensional features per voxel and does not support real-time novel-view feature field rendering, as acknowledged in the limitations.

The effective resolution of upsampled foundation model features remains constrained (effective resolution around 256), leading to slightly degraded performance on scenes with very dense, miniature clutter (e.g., the figurines scene on LERF).
Minor presentation issues, such as template artifacts ('Abbreviated paper title' in the running headers) and minor indexing typos in the supplementary cross-references.

strengths: Clear motivation and problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies two fundamental pain points in current 3DGS-based language fields—spatial ambiguity/bleeding caused by unstructured, overlapping Gaussians, and severe computational/memory overhead incurred by multi-level SAM mask extraction.

Principled integration of Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster): Shifting from 3DGS to disjoint sparse voxels enables deterministic, depth-bounded volume fusion without requiring global depth-sorting or inverse alpha-blending, allowing O(1) memory spatial batching and eliminating severe RAM bottlenecks.

Geometric regularization and confidence gating: Enhancing SVRaster with patch-wise depth, surface normal consistency, and multi-level TSDF depth confidence gating effectively stabilizes the underlying voxel geometry and prevents noisy feature projection.

Efficient multi-level semantics via agglomerative features: Leveraging the dense token-level language alignment of AM-RADIO, together with sliding-window upsampling and self-correcting attention filtering, successfully eliminates the need for expensive multi-scale SAM feature generation while reducing preprocessing time by >8x.

Impressive empirical performance: LESV achieves remarkable gains on open-vocabulary 3D point cloud segmentation on ScanNet (+21.56% mIoU on the 19-class split over Dr. Splat) and ScanNet200 (+12.77% mIoU), while remaining highly competitive on LERF 3D and 2D retrieval benchmarks with a fraction of the compute and memory footprint.

Thorough ablations: The ablation studies effectively disentangle the improvements from the structured geometry/regularization versus the feature backbone (Tables 4 and 5), as well as validating the upsampling scheme against learned upsamplers (Table 8).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty consists primarily of combining existing components: While the system design is well-executed, several individual technical components are borrowed from existing literature (SVRaster for voxel rendering, DN-Gaussian for patch depth loss, MonoSDF for normal supervision, AM-RADIO for backbone features, and SCRA/SCGA filtering from RADSeg).

Feature resolution bottlenecks on small objects: As acknowledged in the limitations, the effective spatial resolution of upsampled VFM features is constrained (around 256x256), which impairs performance on scenes with fine, cluttered objects (e.g., lower mIoU on the 'figurines' scene compared to Dr. Splat in Table 1).

Lack of direct real-time feature rendering: Unlike distillation-based 3DGS methods (e.g., LangSplat, Feature-3DGS) that can render high-dimensional feature fields or low-dimensional autoencoder latents at interactive framerates, LESV focuses on 3D-native querying and requires projecting 3D relevance scores back to 2D views for 2D tasks.

Minor presentation inconsistencies: References to 'cf. supplementary' are sprinkled throughout the text (e.g., pages 6, 8, 15, 16) even though the appendix is appended directly within the same PDF. Additionally, some table headers alternate between 'Acc@25' and 'Acc@025' or 'mAcc'.

strengths: Compelling motivation and paradigm shift: The paper convincingly argues against using unstructured, overlapping 3D Gaussian Splats (3DGS) for direct 3D feature registration due to spatial bleeding and memory bottlenecks. Adopting Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) provides an explicit, disjoint geometry that enables deterministic, spatially batched 3D feature fusion.

Well-motivated geometric regularization: SVRaster often suffers from noisy or fragmented surfaces; regularizing it with patch-wise monocular depth, surface normals, and multi-level TSDF confidence filtering effectively stabilizes surface geometry and prevents false feature projections.

Efficient resolution of multi-level semantic ambiguity: By utilizing the emergent dense language alignment in the AM-RADIO foundation model, the method bypasses the expensive multi-scale SAM segmentation pipelines used by prior works (e.g., LangSplat, LaGa), drastically reducing preprocessing time (from ~120 mins to ~14 mins) while retaining part-to-whole semantic awareness.

Strong empirical performance: LESV achieves a substantial improvement on ScanNet open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation (+21.56% mIoU on the 19-class benchmark over Dr. Splat) and competitive results on LERF 3D object retrieval (85.21% Acc@25).

Thorough ablations and efficiency analysis: Tables 4, 5, and 8 systematically disentangle the contributions of the geometric representation vs. the feature backbone (CLIP vs. AM-RADIO) and validate the feature upsampling scheme. The peak memory analysis (Table 6) clearly shows the scalability benefits over 3DGS registration baselines.
weaknesses: Algorithmic component novelty is somewhat composite: Several core components are direct adaptations of existing techniques—SVRaster for rendering, patch-wise depth and normal losses from MonoSDF/DN-Gaussian, and token filtering (SCRA/SCGA) from RADSeg. The contribution lies predominantly in the cohesive integration and adaptation of these tools to 3D language fields rather than fundamentally new mathematical formulations.

Lack of real-time 2D novel-view feature rendering: Unlike feature field distillation frameworks (e.g., LangSplat, Feature 3DGS), direct voxel registration does not natively support real-time high-dimensional feature splatting/rendering from arbitrary novel viewpoints without first projecting or query-thresholding in 3D.

Performance trade-offs on specific scenes: On the LERF benchmark (Table 1), LESV underperforms Dr. Splat on the waldo_kitchen scene (43.84% vs. 52.00% mIoU), and on figurines in Table 2, which appears related to the current spatial resolution ceiling (~256) of the upsampled VFM features for dense/small objects as acknowledged in the limitations.

Sensitivity of 3D point cloud transfer: The evaluation on ScanNet point clouds relies on transferring voxel features to mesh vertices/points using K-nearest neighbors. Further analysis on sensitivity to the choice of K and voxel resolution would strengthen the claims.
